classification.difficultyReason: The shared task includes quadratic equations in logarithms and equations requiring both negative solutions and original domain exclusions to be preserved.

answer.worked:
Both original arguments are positive when $x\ne0$. Use the quotient law without replacing the even-power logarithms by logarithms of $x$.

$$\begin{align*}\log_2\left(\frac{x^4}{x^2}\right)&=4\\\log_2(x^2)&=4\\x^2&=2^4\\x^2&=16\\x&=\pm4\end{align*}$$

Both values satisfy the original domain.

Both original odd-power arguments require $x>0$.

$$\begin{align*}\log_2(x^2)&=4\\x^2&=2^4\\x^2&=16\\x&=4\end{align*}$$

The negative root is outside the original domain.

The cubic argument requires $x>0$; this also makes the fourth-power argument positive. Applying the quotient law gives

$$\begin{align*}\log_5(x)&=-1\\x&=5^{-1}\\x&=\frac15\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=e$

For $x>0$, use $\ln(x^2)=2\ln x$ and factor the resulting quadratic.
answer.worked:
The first logarithm requires $x>0$, so $\ln(x^2)=2\ln x$.

$$\begin{align*}(\ln x)^2-2\ln x+1&=0\\(\ln x-1)^2&=0\\\ln x&=1\\x&=e\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=9$ or $x=27$.

Use the power law, then factor the quadratic in $\log_3 x$.
answer.worked:
The original domain is $x>0$, so $\log_3(x^5)=5\log_3 x$.

$$\begin{align*}(\log_3 x)^2-5\log_3 x+6&=0\\(\log_3 x-2)(\log_3 x-3)&=0\\\log_3 x&=2\text{ or }3\\x&=9\text{ or }27\end{align*}$$

Both values are positive.

answer.short:
$x=-3$ or $x=1$.

Rewrite the fourth power as the square of $(x+1)^2$ to retain both possible signs of $x+1$.
answer.worked:
The original domain is $x\ne-1$. Since $(x+1)^2>0$, the power law gives $\log_2((x+1)^4)=2\log_2((x+1)^2)$.

$$\begin{align*}3\log_2((x+1)^2)+4\log_2((x+1)^2)&=14\\7\log_2((x+1)^2)&=14\\\log_2((x+1)^2)&=2\\(x+1)^2&=4\\x+1&=\pm2\\x&=-3\text{ or }1\end{align*}$$

Both values satisfy the original domain.

answer.short:
$x=-8$.

For $x<1$, combine the logarithms to obtain $(1-x)^3=729$.
answer.worked:
The original arguments require $(x-1)^2>0$ and $1-x>0$, giving the common domain $x<1$.

$$\begin{align*}\log_3\bigl((x^2-2x+1)(1-x)\bigr)&=6\\\log_3((1-x)^3)&=6\\(1-x)^3&=729\\1-x&=9\\x&=-8\end{align*}$$

The value $-8$ satisfies $x<1$.

answer.short:
$x=-1$ or $x=-\frac73$.

Use the quotient law to obtain $4(x+2)^2=(x+3)^2$, then solve and check both domain exclusions.
answer.worked:
The original squared arguments require $x\ne-2$ and $x\ne-3$.

$$\begin{align*}\log_4\left(\frac{(x+2)^2}{(x+3)^2}\right)&=-1\\\frac{(x+2)^2}{(x+3)^2}&=\frac14\\4(x+2)^2&=(x+3)^2\\4x^2+16x+16&=x^2+6x+9\\3x^2+10x+7&=0\\(3x+7)(x+1)&=0\\x&=-\frac73\text{ or }-1\end{align*}$$

Neither value is excluded from the original domain.
